# ADR-0006: Timestamp Auditing via Spring Data JPA Auditing

## Status

Accepted

⸻

## Context

Every persistent entity in MyFitnessLog includes two auditing timestamps (see DATABASE.md):

* createdAt — set once when the record is first created and never changed.
* updatedAt — set on creation and updated on every subsequent modification.

DATABASE.md also specifies:

* All timestamps are stored in UTC.
* All primary keys are UUIDs generated by the application layer.
* Both timestamp columns already carry a database default of the current timestamp in V1__Initial_schema.sql.

Because these two fields appear on all eight entities, the mechanism that populates them must be consistent, hard to forget, and free of per-entity boilerplate. Three approaches were considered:

1. Spring Data JPA Auditing (@CreatedDate, @LastModifiedDate, AuditingEntityListener, @EnableJpaAuditing).
2. JPA lifecycle callbacks (@PrePersist, @PreUpdate) implemented per entity or in a base class.
3. Manual assignment of timestamps in service or repository code.

⸻

## Decision

MyFitnessLog uses Spring Data JPA Auditing to manage createdAt and updatedAt.

The mechanism is centralized:

* A single abstract base class, AbstractAuditableEntity, is annotated as a @MappedSuperclass and carries the createdAt and updatedAt fields with @CreatedDate and @LastModifiedDate, plus @EntityListeners(AuditingEntityListener.class).
* JPA auditing is activated once through @EnableJpaAuditing in a configuration class.
* All domain entities extend AbstractAuditableEntity and therefore inherit identical auditing behavior.

Timestamps are populated by the application layer at persist and update time.

Ownership of timestamp management is defined as follows:

* Spring Data JPA Auditing is the authoritative mechanism for managing createdAt and updatedAt during normal application execution. All application reads and writes rely on the values it produces.
* The database DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP values on createdAt and updatedAt exist only as a defensive database-level safeguard for inserts performed outside JPA (for example raw SQL or manual data fixes).
* The database defaults are not part of the application's auditing strategy. They must never be relied upon by application code and exist purely as a last-resort safety net.

Identifier generation is intentionally out of scope for this decision. UUID primary keys continue to be generated in the application layer as defined in DATABASE.md and are not managed by the auditing base class.

⸻

## Consequences

### Benefits

* Consistent createdAt and updatedAt behavior across all entities.
* No timestamp-handling code inside individual entities, services, or repositories.
* A single place to change auditing behavior.
* Idiomatic Spring Boot approach with minimal configuration.
* New entities gain auditing automatically by extending the base class, making it hard to forget.

⸻

Trade-offs

* Introduces one shared base class and one configuration annotation that all entities depend on.
* Auditing values are managed by the persistence context, so operations that bypass JPA (for example raw SQL) will rely on the database defaults rather than the auditing mechanism.

These trade-offs are acceptable because consistency and low boilerplate outweigh the small amount of shared infrastructure.

⸻

## Alternatives Considered

JPA Lifecycle Callbacks (@PrePersist / @PreUpdate)

Rejected because:

* The callback logic must be repeated per entity or duplicated in a base class.
* It reimplements, by hand, behavior that Spring Data JPA Auditing already provides.
* It is more error-prone and less idiomatic.

### Manual Assignment

Rejected because:

* Timestamps would be set explicitly in service or repository code.
* It produces the most boilerplate and the highest risk of inconsistency.
* It violates DRY and leaks a persistence concern into the service layer.

⸻

## Implementation Notes

* AbstractAuditableEntity is a @MappedSuperclass; it is not a table and defines no primary key.
* createdAt uses @CreatedDate; updatedAt uses @LastModifiedDate.
* The class carries @EntityListeners(AuditingEntityListener.class).

Entity contract (mandatory):

* Domain entities must never assign createdAt directly.
* Domain entities must never assign updatedAt directly.
* Both fields are framework-managed by Spring Data JPA Auditing and are set exclusively through the auditing mechanism.

* @EnableJpaAuditing is declared once in the configuration layer.
* Timestamps are stored in UTC, consistent with DATABASE.md.
* When authentication is introduced in a future version, this mechanism can be extended with @CreatedBy and @LastModifiedBy backed by an AuditorAware implementation, without changing existing entities.

⸻
